dg.cap: FinOps is a loop: see and attribute the spend, cut usage first, then rates, then govern and repeat.

cloud-finops.md:
## Why it exists
The cloud turned infrastructure spend from a yearly procurement decision into something every engineer changes with a pull request. A forgotten test cluster, a chatty NAT gateway or an unbounded log pipeline can add thousands to a monthly bill before anyone notices. **FinOps** is the practice of making cloud cost visible, attributable and optimizable, so engineering, finance and product decide together where the money should go.

The goal is not "spend less". It is **spend deliberately**: know who spends what, why, and whether it buys value. The FinOps Foundation's framework describes a loop of three phases that repeat: **Inform** (visibility and allocation), **Optimize** (rates and usage) and **Operate** (governance and culture).

{{dg:0}}

## Where the bill comes from
| Cost driver | Typical surprise | First question to ask |
|---|---|---|
| **Compute** (VMs, containers, functions) | Idle or oversized instances, always-on non-prod | What is CPU and memory utilization at the 95th percentile? |
| **Storage** | Snapshots, old object versions, unattached disks, hot-tier data nobody reads | When was it last read? |
| **Data transfer** | Cross-AZ and cross-region traffic, NAT gateway processing, internet egress | Which flows cross a billing boundary? |
| **Managed data services** | Over-provisioned databases and clusters, per-GB ingestion in logs and metrics | Are we paying for capacity or for use? |
| **Licenses and marketplace** | Per-core or per-seat software on large instances | Is there a cheaper edition or a managed alternative? |
| **AI and GPUs** | Idle accelerators, large models for easy tasks, uncapped token spend | What does one request cost, and who owns the budget? |

## Inform: allocation is the foundation
You cannot optimize what you cannot attribute. Build three layers:
1. **Account and subscription structure.** Separate production from non-production and give big teams their own accounts, so the bill itself says a lot (see the landing zone lesson).
2. **Tags and labels.** A small mandatory set (`team`, `service`, `env`, `cost-center`) enforced by policy at creation time. Tags must be activated for cost reporting (in AWS, as cost allocation tags) and only apply from that point forward.
3. **Shared cost rules.** Kubernetes clusters, shared databases and networking serve many teams. Decide a documented split (by requests, by usage, by headcount) and apply it consistently.

Showback (report what each team spent) comes first; chargeback (actually bill the team) only when the data is trusted.

### One schema for every vendor: FOCUS
The FinOps Foundation's **FOCUS** (FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification) defines a common schema for billing data so AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and SaaS exports can be queried the same way. Core columns include `BilledCost`, `EffectiveCost` (amortized, with commitment purchases spread over their term), `ListCost`, `ChargeCategory`, `PricingCategory`, `ServiceName`, `SubAccountId`, `ResourceId`, `ChargePeriodStart` and `Tags`.

```sql
-- DuckDB over FOCUS-format Parquet exports: monthly effective cost by team tag and service
SELECT date_trunc('month', ChargePeriodStart)              AS month,
       coalesce(json_extract_string(Tags, '$.team'), '(untagged)') AS team,
       ServiceName,
       round(sum(EffectiveCost), 2)                        AS effective_cost
FROM read_parquet('focus/*.parquet')
WHERE ChargeCategory = 'Usage'
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY month, effective_cost DESC;
```
Track the **untagged share** itself as a metric. It is the best single indicator of allocation health.

## Optimize: two levers, rate and usage
**Usage optimization** means paying for less: delete the idle, right-size the oversized, schedule the intermittent.
**Rate optimization** means paying less per unit of what you keep: commitments and cheaper capacity types.

Do usage first. Committing to capacity you are about to shrink locks in waste.

### Usage levers
| Lever | How | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| **Rightsizing** | Compare provisioned vs observed CPU, memory, IOPS over weeks; use provider recommenders as a starting point | Peaks, month-end jobs, memory-bound workloads |
| **Scheduling** | Stop dev and test environments nights and weekends | Startup time, stateful systems |
| **Autoscaling** | Scale on demand; scale to zero where supported | Cold starts, scale-in disruption |
| **Storage tiering and lifecycle** | Lifecycle rules to cheaper tiers, expire old versions, delete orphan snapshots and volumes | Retrieval fees and minimum durations |
| **Newer generations** | Move to newer instance families (including Arm: Graviton on AWS, Ampere or Cobalt on Azure) and newer volume types | Needs a compatibility test |
| **Kubernetes bin-packing** | Right-size requests, use a node autoscaler such as Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler, consolidate nodes | Requests set far above use waste most clusters |
| **Data transfer design** | Keep chatty services in one AZ or region, use VPC endpoints for AWS service traffic, cache and compress | Availability trade-offs of single-AZ |

### Rate levers
| Option | Discount idea | Commitment | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **On-demand** | None | None | Highest unit price |
| **Savings Plans / Azure savings plans** | Commit to an hourly spend for 1 or 3 years; flexible across sizes, sometimes services | Spend per hour | Paying for unused commitment |
| **Reserved instances / reservations** | Commit to specific capacity | Specific SKU | Less flexible, can often be exchanged or sold depending on the provider |
| **Spot / preemptible / Azure Spot** | Spare capacity at a deep discount | None | Interruptions; needs fault-tolerant design |
| **Negotiated enterprise discounts and private pricing** | Volume-based | Contract | Only at scale |

#### The break-even rule for commitments
A commitment gives a discount `d` on the usage it covers, but you pay for it whether you use it or not. It beats on-demand only if you use more than `(1 - d)` of it. With a 28 percent discount the commitment must be at least 72 percent utilized.

```python
def commitment_breakeven_utilization(discount: float) -> float:
    """Minimum share of a commitment you must use to match on-demand cost."""
    return 1.0 - discount


def commitment_savings(committed_per_hour: float, discount: float, on_demand_usage_per_hour: float) -> float:
    """Hourly saving vs pure on-demand. `on_demand_usage_per_hour` is eligible usage priced at on-demand rates."""
    covered_value = committed_per_hour / (1.0 - discount)       # on-demand value the commitment can absorb
    covered_used = min(on_demand_usage_per_hour, covered_value)  # you cannot use more than exists
    return covered_used - committed_per_hour                     # on-demand cost avoided minus what you pay


# 28% discount on a $10/hour commitment absorbs ~$13.89/hour of on-demand usage
assert round(commitment_savings(10, 0.28, 13.89), 2) == 3.89   # fully used: saves
assert commitment_savings(10, 0.28, 7.2) == -2.8                # only 7.2 used: loses money
```
Commit to a **floor** (usage you are confident will exist in a year), not your peak, and ladder purchases over time instead of buying once.

## Operate: unit economics, budgets and anomalies
- **Unit cost** ties spend to value: cost per request, per active user, per order, per 1,000 inferences. A rising bill with a falling unit cost is healthy growth; a flat bill with a rising unit cost is a problem.
- **Budgets and alerts** at the account, team and tag level, on both actual and forecast spend.
- **Anomaly detection** catches runaway spend within a day, not at month end.
- **Regular reviews** with engineering: top movers, top savings opportunities, commitment coverage and utilization.

A simple, explainable anomaly rule that works without any vendor tool:

```python
from statistics import median


def cost_anomalies(daily_costs, window=14, threshold=4.0):
    """Flag days whose cost is far above the recent median, using a robust (MAD) spread."""
    flagged = []
    for i in range(window, len(daily_costs)):
        hist = daily_costs[i - window:i]
        med = median(hist)
        mad = max(median(abs(x - med) for x in hist), 0.01 * med, 0.01)   # floor: a flat history must not make a $1 change look infinite
        score = (daily_costs[i] - med) / (1.4826 * mad)
        if score > threshold:
            flagged.append((i, daily_costs[i], round(score, 1)))
    return flagged
```
A budget as code with Terraform (a forecast alert at 80 percent for one team's tag):

```hcl
resource "aws_budgets_budget" "payments_monthly" {
  name         = "payments-monthly"
  budget_type  = "COST"
  limit_amount = "5000"
  limit_unit   = "USD"
  time_unit    = "MONTHLY"

  cost_filter {
    name   = "TagKeyValue"
    values = ["user:team$payments"]
  }

  notification {
    comparison_operator        = "GREATER_THAN"
    threshold                  = 80
    threshold_type             = "PERCENTAGE"
    notification_type          = "FORECASTED"
    subscriber_email_addresses = ["payments-leads@example.com"]
  }
}
```

## Kubernetes cost
The cluster bill is one line item; the question is which team or service caused it. **OpenCost** (a CNCF project) and tools built on it allocate node, storage and network cost to namespaces, labels and workloads using resource requests and usage. The lever that matters most is **requests versus actual use**: pods that request 4 CPUs and use 0.3 force you to buy nodes for the request.

## Who does what
| Role | Owns |
|---|---|
| **Engineering** | Architecture and usage decisions, tagging, acting on recommendations |
| **FinOps / platform** | Data, tooling, allocation rules, commitment strategy, reviews |
| **Finance** | Budgets, forecasting, accounting treatment of commitments |
| **Product and leadership** | Which spend is worth it; unit-cost targets |

> [!pitfall] Buying commitments before cleaning up. You lock in a discount on waste. Rightsize and delete first, then commit to the stable floor.
> [!pitfall] Treating the cheapest option as the goal. A cheaper region, tier or instance that raises latency, risk or engineer time can cost more overall. Optimize cost per unit of value.
> [!pitfall] Tags that exist but are unreliable. Enforce them at creation (policy, IaC modules) and measure the untagged percentage, or reports will be wrong and teams will not trust them.
> [!pitfall] Ignoring data transfer and NAT costs until the bill arrives. They are invisible in architecture diagrams and large in practice; model them in design reviews.
> [!pitfall] Spot instances for stateful or interruption-intolerant work without handling the interruption notice.
> [!pitfall] Confusing billed cost with effective (amortized) cost. A big upfront purchase makes the billed month look terrible and later months look free; use effective cost for comparison.
> [!tip] Put the cost estimate in the pull request. Tools such as Infracost show the monthly cost change of Terraform changes before merge.
> [!tip] Start with a few high-value dashboards (spend by team, untagged share, commitment coverage and utilization, top 10 movers) rather than a hundred charts.
> [!cost] Free to ignore, expensive to forget: logs and metrics ingestion, cross-AZ traffic, idle load balancers and IPs, old snapshots, forgotten test clusters and idle GPUs.
> [!security] Cost data reveals architecture and customers. Restrict billing and cost-explorer access, and treat exported billing buckets like production data.
> [!prod] Give every team a named cost owner, a monthly review, and the authority to act. Visibility without ownership changes nothing.
> [!version] Verified 2026-10-20: the FOCUS specification's own site lists 1.4 as the latest version (ratified June 4, 2026) after 1.3 (December 2025). The columns used here (`BilledCost`, `EffectiveCost`, `ListCost`, `ChargeCategory`, `PricingCategory`, `SubAccountId`, `Tags`) appear in the FOCUS changelog and in Microsoft's FOCUS schema page, where `Tags` is a JSON object; `AmortizedCost` and `ChargeType` were the pre-1.0 names. The AWS Budgets tag filter format `user:TagKey$TagValue` (the tag must be an activated cost allocation tag) is confirmed by several Terraform examples and AWS re:Post. The commitment helper (with its asserts) and the anomaly helper were run locally on synthetic numbers; the anomaly helper had a bug on perfectly flat cost history (a $1 change scored about 674 million), now fixed with a floor on the spread. NOT verified: the exact 1.4 column list was not opened, `ServiceName`, `ResourceId` and `ChargePeriodStart` were not individually confirmed, the DuckDB SQL was never run (no DuckDB offline, and `Tags` may be a string or a map depending on your export), and the Terraform was not planned. Savings plan, reservation and Spot terms and discount sizes change and vary by provider; check current pricing pages.
q: Why should usage optimization come before buying commitments?

A commitment locks in a discount on whatever you currently use. If you buy before deleting idle resources and rightsizing, you pay for waste for the whole term. Commit to the stable floor after cleanup.
At a 28 percent commitment discount, what utilization makes the commitment break even against on-demand?
72 percent (1 minus the discount). Below that you pay for unused commitment and lose money; above it you save.
What is the difference between billed cost and effective cost?

Billed cost is what the invoice shows in the period, including upfront purchases. Effective (amortized) cost spreads commitment purchases over their term, so months are comparable and teams are charged fairly.

cloud-landing-zones.md:
## Why it exists
A single cloud account works for a demo. In a real company it becomes a liability: every team shares one blast radius, permissions are impossible to scope, the bill cannot be split, a compromised key reaches everything, and one runaway workload hits shared service quotas. The standard answer is **many accounts** (AWS accounts, Azure subscriptions, Google Cloud projects) arranged under one organization, with shared guardrails. The pre-built, governed foundation that new workloads land in is called a **landing zone**.

An account is the strongest isolation boundary the provider offers for permissions, billing and quotas. A landing zone makes creating and governing hundreds of them boring and repeatable.

{{dg:0}}

## What a landing zone contains
| Area | What you set up | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Organization structure** | A hierarchy: AWS Organizations OUs, Azure management groups | Attach policy once, inherit everywhere |
| **Identity** | One identity provider, SSO, short-lived role access (IAM Identity Center on AWS, Entra ID on Azure), break-glass accounts | No long-lived human keys, central joiner-mover-leaver |
| **Guardrails** | Preventive policy (SCPs, Azure Policy deny), detective policy (Config rules, Policy audit) | Rules that hold whatever a workload team does |
| **Logging and audit** | Organization-wide audit trail to a locked-down log account; configuration history | Evidence and forensics that an attacker in a workload account cannot erase |
| **Security tooling** | Delegated admin for threat detection, posture management, vulnerability scanning | One place to see findings across all accounts |
| **Network** | Hub-and-spoke or similar, central egress and inspection, planned address space | Connectivity without overlap or surprise |
| **Account vending** | A pipeline that creates a new account with the baseline already applied | Days of tickets become minutes |
| **Cost structure** | Budgets, tag policy, billing visibility per account | Allocation for FinOps |

## A common AWS account layout
| Account | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Management** | Owns the organization and billing. Almost nothing runs here; SCPs do not apply to it |
| **Log archive** | Receives organization CloudTrail and config logs, write-once storage, tight access |
| **Security tooling / audit** | Delegated administrator for GuardDuty, Security Hub, Config aggregation, Inspector |
| **Network** | Transit gateway, shared VPCs or inspection VPC, DNS, egress |
| **Shared services** | CI/CD runners, artifact registries, internal tools, IPAM |
| **Workload accounts** | One per application and environment (for example `shop-prod`, `shop-staging`), grouped in OUs such as Prod, NonProd, Sandbox |

Azure expresses the same idea with **management groups** (Platform: identity, management, connectivity; Landing Zones: corp and online; Sandbox; Decommissioned) and **subscriptions** as the account-like unit, with Azure Policy attached at management group level.

## Guardrails: SCPs, the preventive layer
A **Service Control Policy** sets the maximum permissions any identity in an account can ever have, whatever its IAM policies say. It filters; it never grants. It applies to every account below where it is attached, except the management account.

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyLeavingTheOrganization",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "organizations:LeaveOrganization",
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyRootUserActions",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "*",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:root" } }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ProtectOrganizationTrail",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": ["cloudtrail:StopLogging", "cloudtrail:DeleteTrail", "cloudtrail:UpdateTrail"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:cloudtrail:*:*:trail/org-trail"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyOutsideApprovedRegions",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "NotAction": ["iam:*", "organizations:*", "sts:*", "support:*", "budgets:*", "ce:*", "cloudfront:*", "route53:*"],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": { "StringNotEquals": { "aws:RequestedRegion": ["eu-west-1", "eu-central-1"] } }
    }
  ]
}
```
The region deny excludes global services (IAM, Organizations, STS and similar) whose API calls are not regional; without that `NotAction` list you can lock out basic operations.

The same policy-as-guardrail idea on Azure is **Azure Policy** with `deny`, `audit` and `deployIfNotExists` effects (for example: allowed locations, required tags, no public IPs on NICs, diagnostic settings enforced).

## Worked example: an organization in Terraform
```hcl
resource "aws_organizations_organization" "this" {
  feature_set = "ALL"
  aws_service_access_principals = [
    "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com",
    "config.amazonaws.com",
    "sso.amazonaws.com",
  ]
  enabled_policy_types = ["SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY", "TAG_POLICY"]
}

locals {
  root_id = aws_organizations_organization.this.roots[0].id
}

resource "aws_organizations_organizational_unit" "workloads" {
  name      = "Workloads"
  parent_id = local.root_id
}

resource "aws_organizations_organizational_unit" "prod" {
  name      = "Prod"
  parent_id = aws_organizations_organizational_unit.workloads.id
}

resource "aws_organizations_policy" "baseline" {
  name    = "baseline-guardrails"
  type    = "SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY"
  content = file("${path.module}/scp-baseline.json")
}

resource "aws_organizations_policy_attachment" "workloads_baseline" {
  policy_id = aws_organizations_policy.baseline.id
  target_id = aws_organizations_organizational_unit.workloads.id
}

resource "aws_organizations_account" "shop_prod" {
  name      = "shop-prod"
  email     = "aws+shop-prod@example.com"
  parent_id = aws_organizations_organizational_unit.prod.id
  role_name = "OrganizationAccountAccessRole"
  lifecycle { ignore_changes = [role_name] }
}
```
Test SCPs on a sandbox OU first; an overly broad deny can block the very roles you need to fix it. Mind the quotas: an SCP document can be at most 5,120 characters, and at most 5 SCPs can attach to the root, an OU or an account (the effective permissions are the intersection of all of them), so keep policies compact and split by purpose.

## Human access without keys
Use **IAM Identity Center** (AWS) or **Entra ID with PIM** (Azure): people sign in with the company identity provider and receive short-lived role sessions per account through **permission sets** or role assignments. Map groups to roles (for example `Platform-Admins` get admin in the platform accounts; developers get read-write in non-prod and read-only plus a request-based elevation in prod). Keep two emergency break-glass identities with hardware MFA, store their credentials offline, and alert on any use.

## Networking
- **Plan address space centrally.** Overlapping CIDRs make peering and transit impossible later. Use an IPAM (AWS VPC IPAM, Azure IPAM tooling or a documented spreadsheet in Git) and allocate non-overlapping ranges per account and region.
- **Hub-and-spoke:** workload VPCs and VNets attach to a hub (AWS Transit Gateway, Azure Virtual WAN or a hub VNet) that centralizes egress, inspection and on-premises links.
- **Central egress** reduces public addresses but adds a cost and a choke point; model NAT and transit data-processing charges.
- **Private connectivity to services** (VPC endpoints, private endpoints) keeps traffic off the internet and often cuts transfer costs.
- **DNS:** decide early who owns zones, private resolution and cross-account sharing.

## Account vending
New teams should get a ready account in minutes, with the baseline applied: logging, security agents, network attachment, budgets, tags, an admin role for the owning team, and SSO assignments.

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **AWS Control Tower** | Managed landing zone: sets up the organization structure, a log archive and audit setup, controls (guardrails) and an Account Factory |
| **Account Factory for Terraform (AFT)** | A Terraform pipeline that provisions Control Tower accounts and runs customizations |
| **Custom with Organizations and Terraform** | Full control and more work; common in mature platform teams |
| **Azure landing zone reference architecture and accelerators** | Microsoft's pattern and Infrastructure-as-Code modules for management groups, policy, connectivity and subscription vending |

## Decisions to make early
| Question | Guidance |
|---|---|
| How many accounts? | One per workload and environment is a solid default; avoid hundreds of tiny accounts before automation exists, but never put prod and non-prod together |
| Single region or multi-region? | Start with approved regions in the SCP; add regions deliberately |
| Who is the platform team? | Own the landing zone as a product with versioned releases |
| How do changes ship? | Everything as code, reviewed, applied by a pipeline with a narrowly scoped role |
| How do you decommission? | A documented process: suspend, retain logs, close account, update inventory |

> [!pitfall] Running workloads in the management account. It cannot be restricted by SCPs and holds the keys to the whole organization. Keep it for governance and billing only.
> [!pitfall] An SCP that locks you out. Test on a sandbox OU, keep break-glass access, and remember an SCP only denies; the missing allow in IAM is a separate problem.
> [!pitfall] Overlapping IP ranges. Fixing them after teams have deployed means re-addressing production. Allocate from a central plan from day one.
> [!pitfall] Editing resources that a managed landing zone owns. Changes outside the supported path cause drift and failed updates; use the documented customization mechanism.
> [!pitfall] Too much, too soon. A complete enterprise landing zone before the first team has shipped produces process nobody follows. Ship a small baseline and grow it with real needs.
> [!pitfall] Forgetting global services in region-deny policies, then wondering why IAM, CloudFront or Route 53 calls fail.
> [!security] Protect the log archive: separate account, object lock or write-once retention, no delete rights for workload admins, and alerts on any change to the audit trail.
> [!security] Use short-lived role sessions for people and OIDC federation for CI/CD. Long-lived access keys in repos are the usual breach path.
> [!cost] Central egress, transit gateways, inspection firewalls and per-account security tooling all add recurring charges. Budget for them and tag the platform accounts so the shared cost can be allocated.
> [!tip] Keep an account inventory (id, owner, environment, data classification, creation date, cost center) as data, generated from the organization, and use it in access reviews and cost reports.
> [!prod] Version the landing zone and test changes in a sandbox organization or OU before rolling to production OUs. Announce SCP changes; they can break teams without warning.
> [!version] Verified 2026-10-20 from AWS and Microsoft documentation: AWS Control Tower landing zone version 4.0 no longer requires a Security OU, lets you define your own organizational structure, makes the service integrations (AWS Config, AWS CloudTrail, SecurityRoles, AWS Backup) optional, and sends drift notifications to EventBridge in the management account instead of SNS when the full baseline is not enabled. The SCP limits (5,120 characters per document, 5 SCPs per root, OU or account) match the AWS Organizations quotas page. The Azure management group names (Platform with Connectivity, Identity and Management; Landing Zones with Corp and Online; Sandbox; Decommissioned) match the Azure Landing Zones project, whose newer Bicep and Terraform accelerators also show a Security group under Platform; the Azure landing zones page link was found by search. The SCP JSON was checked as valid JSON. NOT verified: the Terraform was never planned or applied, the Control Tower 4.0 details were not re-opened this time, and the SCP statements were not tested in a real organization.
q: What does a Service Control Policy do, and what can it not do?
It sets the maximum permissions for accounts under the OU where it is attached, filtering what IAM could allow. It never grants permissions, and it does not apply to the management account.
Why keep workloads out of the management account?
It owns the organization and billing, and SCPs cannot restrict it. A compromise or mistake there affects every account, so it should only be used for governance.
Why plan IP address ranges centrally in a multi-account setup?
Overlapping CIDR blocks cannot be peered or routed through a shared hub. Fixing overlaps after teams deploy means re-addressing production networks.

cloud-rosetta.md:
## Why it exists
Every cloud sells the same building blocks under different names. Learn the ideas once and the vocabulary of AWS, Azure and Google Cloud becomes a translation exercise instead of three separate subjects.

{{dg:0}}

## Core ideas
- **Regions and Availability Zones:** a Region is a geographic area, and the zones inside it are separate data centers. Deploy across zones for availability, and pick Regions for latency, price and data-residency rules.
- **Service models:** IaaS (virtual machines), PaaS (managed runtimes and databases), FaaS (functions) and SaaS (finished software).
- **Shared responsibility:** the provider secures the cloud itself, and you secure what you put in it: identities, data and configuration.
- **Pricing:** pay as you go, commitments (Savings Plans, reservations) for discounts, and spot capacity for interruptible work. Data leaving the cloud is billed.
- **Elasticity:** scale out and in with demand instead of buying for peak.

## The Rosetta stone
| Need | AWS | Azure |
|---|---|---|
| Virtual machines | EC2 | Virtual Machines |
| Serverless functions | Lambda | Azure Functions (Flex Consumption) |
| Containers, no servers | ECS on Fargate | Container Apps |
| Kubernetes | EKS | AKS |
| Object storage | S3 | Blob Storage |
| Managed Postgres | RDS and Aurora | Azure Database for PostgreSQL |
| NoSQL | DynamoDB | Cosmos DB |
| Queues and events | SQS, SNS, EventBridge | Service Bus, Event Grid |
| Private network | VPC | Virtual Network (VNet) |
| Load balancing | ALB | Application Gateway, Front Door |
| Identity | IAM, Identity Center | Microsoft Entra ID, Azure RBAC |
| Secrets and keys | Secrets Manager, KMS | Key Vault |
| Monitoring | CloudWatch, X-Ray | Azure Monitor, Application Insights |
| Infrastructure as code | CloudFormation, CDK | Bicep, ARM templates |
| LLMs and AI | Bedrock, SageMaker | Azure OpenAI and AI Foundry, Azure Machine Learning |
| Account structure | Organizations and accounts | Management groups and subscriptions |

Terraform works on both clouds, which is why many teams use it to avoid learning two infrastructure-as-code languages.

## How to choose
Pick the cloud your company, customers or data already use. Skills transfer between clouds: networking, identity, least privilege, infrastructure as code and observability matter more than any single console.

> [!tip] Learn one cloud well, then use this table to translate. The concepts (identity, networks, storage tiers, scaling, cost) repeat everywhere.
> [!pitfall] Treating the cloud as someone else's data center. Lifting servers over unchanged usually costs more and gains little.
> [!security] Shared responsibility means a managed service can still be breached through your misconfiguration, such as a public bucket or an over-permissive role.
q: Who is responsible for a public storage bucket that leaks data?
You are: configuration of the service and the data in it fall on the customer under shared responsibility.
What is the Azure equivalent of an AWS VPC?
